```{r setup}
s <- read.csv("../results/summary.csv")
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
pv <- s[is.finite(s$eps), ]
ig <- pv[pv$method == "private_ignored", ]; pr <- pv[pv$method == "private_propagated", ]
np <- s[s$method == "non_private", ]
use <- ig[ig$eps >= 1 & ig$n_t >= 150, ]
cell <- function(d, n, e, r, m) d[d$n_t == n & d$eps == e & d$release == r & d$em == m, ]
w <- merge(ig[, c("cell", "width")], pr[, c("cell", "width")], by = "cell", suffixes = c("_i", "_p"))
w$share <- 1 - (w$width_i / w$width_p)^2; w <- merge(w, ig[, c("cell", "n_t", "eps", "release")])
inf2 <- ig[ig$release == "means_sds", ]
rm2 <- function(n, e, m, r) cell(pr, n, e, r, m)$rmse
nat <- s[!is.finite(s$eps), ]
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

**Background.** A target trial may release its covariate moments under differential
privacy, adding Laplace noise whose variance the data holder knows exactly. Catalog
problem ADJ-15 asks whether MAIC to noisy moments needs that noise propagated, and
whether releasing more moments is worth its share of the privacy budget.

**Methods.** MAIC of a source trial (200 per arm) to a target of 40, 150 or 500
patients releasing means, or means and second moments, at budgets
$\varepsilon \in \{0.5, 1, 4\}$ or without privacy; linear or quadratic effect
modification; 48 scenarios, 1000 replicates each. Intervals ignored the noise or added
$\hat g^\top\Sigma_{\text{noise}}\hat g$.

**Results.** At budgets of at least 1 and targets of at least 150, ignoring the noise
gave coverage as low as `r f3(min(use$coverage))`; at 40 patients it fell to
`r f3(min(ig$coverage[ig$n_t == 40]))`. The noise share of the variance ranged from
under 0.01 to `r f3(max(w$share))`. Adding the known noise variance restored coverage
to at least `r f3(min(pr$coverage))` in every private scenario, conservatively where
noise dominated. Releasing second moments at small targets and budgets left no feasible
weights in up to `r f3(max(inf2$infeasible))` of replicates, because noisy second
moments fell below the squared means or outside the source data.

**Conclusion.** The noise is not negligible at usable budgets for trial-sized targets.
Its variance is a published number, so the correction costs nothing and should always be
applied. Extra moments pay only at larger budgets or targets.

# The problem {#sec-problem}

The Laplace mechanism releases a statistic with sensitivity $\Delta$ plus noise of scale
$\Delta/\varepsilon$ and variance $2(\Delta/\varepsilon)^2$ [@dwork2006]. For a mean over
$n_T$ patients of a covariate clipped to a range of 6, $\Delta = 6/n_T$, so the noise
variance scales as $1/(n_T\varepsilon)^2$ while the sampling variance of the moment
scales as $1/n_T$. MAIC [@signorovitch2010] weights the source to the released moments,
so the estimate moves with the noise by the gradient $g = \partial\hat\Delta/\partial m$.
Unlike other moment uncertainty in population adjustment, $\Sigma_{\text{noise}}$ needs no
estimation.

# Design {#sec-design}

Registered protocol: `protocol.md`; ADEMP structure [@morris2019]. Source A versus C,
two covariates clipped to $[-3, 3]$; $y = 0.5\sum x_j + A(-0.4 + 0.4x_1 + \beta_2x_1^2) + e$,
$\beta_2 \in \{0, 0.3\}$. Target covariates $N(0.5, 0.8^2)$. With second moments
released the budget is split equally over four statistics (sensitivity $9/n_T$ for the
second moments). Truth: the effect at the target trial's own non-private moments.
$\hat g$ by central differences. Replicates whose noisy moments admitted no weights
are counted as infeasible and excluded from coverage.

# Results {#sec-results}

![Coverage of the noise-ignoring and noise-propagating intervals against the share of the propagated variance due to privacy noise. Each point is a scenario.](figures/fig1-coverage.png){#fig-cov}

Coverage of the noise-ignoring interval fell as the noise share grew, and the
propagated interval held nominal or above (@fig-cov). The refuting sentence fails: at
$n_T = 150$, $\varepsilon = 1$, means only, the noise was
`r f3(w$share[w$n_t == 150 & w$eps == 1 & w$release == "means"][1])` to
`r f3(w$share[w$n_t == 150 & w$eps == 1 & w$release == "means"][2])` of the variance and
coverage ignoring it was `r f3(cell(ig, 150, 1, "means", "linear")$coverage)` (linear)
and `r f3(cell(ig, 150, 1, "means", "quadratic")$coverage)` (quadratic); with second
moments also released it was `r f3(cell(ig, 150, 1, "means_sds", "quadratic")$coverage)`.
At $n_T = 500$ or $\varepsilon = 4$ the noise was a few percent of the variance and
could be ignored.

The propagated interval over-covered where noise dominated (up to
`r f3(max(pr$coverage))` at $n_T = 40$). Two causes contribute: the replicates with the
most extreme noise were infeasible and dropped, and a linearization overstates the
movement of an estimate that cannot leave the range of the source data.

Releasing second moments halves each statistic's budget. It paid under quadratic
modification when the budget was large (RMSE `r f3(rm2(150, 4, "quadratic", "means_sds"))`
against `r f3(rm2(150, 4, "quadratic", "means"))` at $n_T = 150$, $\varepsilon = 4$), and
cost accuracy and feasibility when it was small (infeasible in
`r f3(cell(ig, 150, 0.5, "means_sds", "linear")$infeasible)` of replicates at $n_T = 150$,
$\varepsilon = 0.5$). Without privacy the three analyses coincided (coverage
`r f3(min(nat$coverage))` to `r f3(max(nat$coverage))`).

# What this does not answer {#sec-limits}

Laplace mechanism only; the Gaussian mechanism, released correlations and overlap
levels were not varied. Performance is conditional on feasible weights, so at small
budgets with second moments released it describes a minority of replicates. The choice
of budget itself, a governance question, is outside the study. Peer review has not been
done.
